aliases: Massacres of the Jews of the Rhineland during the First Crusade

location: Speyer, Worms, Mainz, Cologne and the surrounding villages, Trier, Metz, Regensburg, and other towns of the Rhineland and the German lands

date.note: The attacks took place in the spring and early summer of 1096 (the Hebrew year 4856, abbreviated tatnav), while crusading contingents were gathering for the expedition proclaimed at Clermont in November 1095. The communities of Speyer (early May), Worms (mid- to late May), and Mainz were attacked in succession; the Hebrew chronicle of Solomon bar Samson dates the massacre at Mainz to 3 Sivan, a Tuesday, which corresponds to 27 May 1096. The Jews of Cologne, dispersed by their archbishop to nearby villages, were attacked there in June.

summary: The Rhineland massacres were attacks in the spring and summer of 1096, during the gathering of the First Crusade, by crusading bands (among them the army of Count Emicho) and in places by local townspeople, on the Jewish communities of Speyer, Worms, Mainz, Cologne, and other towns, in which many Jews were killed, some were baptized under duress, and many chose death, at times by their own hand and the hands of their families, as kiddush ha-shem (sanctification of the divine Name). The events are known from three twelfth-century Hebrew chronicles and from Latin chroniclers, and they became a lasting paradigm of martyrdom in Ashkenazi memory.
description:
In the spring of 1096, as contingents from northern France and Germany assembled for the expedition to Jerusalem preached by Pope Urban II, some of these bands, joined in several towns by local burghers, turned on the Jewish communities of the Rhineland. These communities, at Speyer, Worms, and Mainz above all, were among the oldest and most learned centres of Ashkenazi Jewry; Rashi had studied in the academies of Worms and Mainz a generation earlier. At Speyer in early May the bishop intervened and the losses were limited. At Worms in mid- to late May the Jews who stayed in their homes and those who had taken refuge in the bishop's palace were attacked in two waves. At Mainz, according to the Hebrew chronicle of Solomon bar Samson, the army of 'Emico the wicked, the enemy of the Jews' came against the city on 3 Sivan (27 May 1096); the Jews had sought the protection of Archbishop Ruthard, but 'the bishop's men, who had promised to help them, were the very first to flee'. The Jews of Cologne were dispersed by their archbishop to nearby villages, where they were attacked in June, and violence followed at Trier, Metz, Regensburg, and Prague. Emicho's army itself was halted at the Hungarian border fortress of Wieselburg (Moson) and broke up.

The Latin chroniclers record the attacks from the Christian side. Albert of Aachen reports that the attackers acted 'in a spirit of cruelty against the Jewish people', 'asserting it to be the beginning of their expedition and their duty against the enemies of the Christian faith', and that at Mainz they 'killed the Jews, about seven hundred in number', who had 'fled in hope of safety to Bishop Rothard'; he condemns the killing as done 'through greed of money, rather than for the sake of God's justice' and reads the army's collapse in Hungary as divine judgment. Ekkehard of Aura says that Emicho led 'almost twelve thousand cross bearers' and that the crusaders either destroyed the Jews 'or forced them into the bosom of the Church'. The Hebrew chronicles, for their part, attribute to the attackers the motive of vengeance for the Crucifixion: at Mainz, in Solomon bar Samson's account, once the gate was opened 'the enemies of the Lord said to each other', 'Now let us avenge the blood of "the hanged one" [Jesus]', the bracketed gloss being the translator's. The numbers differ between the sources: for Mainz, Solomon bar Samson reports that 'on one day, on the third of Siwan, on a Tuesday eleven hundred souls were killed and slaughtered', while Albert gives about seven hundred; both figures are reported here as their authors' own.

The Hebrew narratives centre on the Jews' response. According to the Hebrew narratives, faced with the choice of baptism or death, some accepted baptism under duress, while many chose death as kiddush ha-shem, the sanctification of the divine Name, at times killing their own children and themselves rather than fall into the attackers' hands. Solomon bar Samson presents the martyrs as resolving 'to kill ourselves for the unity of His holy name', describes how 'they tied their sons as Abraham tied Isaac his son', and places them beside 'Rabbi Akiba and his companions'; the Latin Albert also records that 'mothers cut the throats of nursing children with knives'. In 1097 Emperor Henry IV permitted Jews who had been forcibly baptized to return to Judaism. Three Hebrew accounts survive, the chronicle attributed to Solomon bar Samson (written around 1140), the chronicle of Eliezer bar Nathan, and the anonymous Mainz narrative (the 'Narrative of the Old Persecutions'), together with liturgical poems (piyyutim and kinot) and memorial lists of the dead; they were critically edited by Eva Haverkamp in 2005.

Historians interpret these texts differently. Robert Chazan reads the chronicles as substantially reliable reports shaped by religious purpose, and traces the violence to radical popular notions of crusading as vengeance, held by some bands but not by the ecclesiastical and imperial authorities who in several places tried to protect the Jews. Jeremy Cohen reads the same narratives as twelfth-century constructions of memory that say as much about their authors as about the martyrs, revealing alongside their praise of martyrdom the doubts and guilt of survivors who had submitted, at least temporarily, to baptism. The relationship and dating of the three chronicles are also debated. The memory of 1096 shaped later Ashkenazi responses to persecution: the Hebrew account of the Second Crusade by Ephraim of Bonn, for example, records the violence of 1146-1147, the opposition of Bernard of Clairvaux to the anti-Jewish preaching of the monk Radulf, and an attack on Rabbenu Tam at Ramerupt.
editorial_notes: This entry is filed under judaism as a storage convention per ADR-0010, because it concerns violence against Jewish communities and is filed with the targeted community; the filing is not a claim that the event belongs to one tradition. The crusade within which the attacks occurred is linked by relation (first-crusade). NEUTRALITY: both sides are presented in their own voices, the Jewish communities through the Hebrew chronicle of Solomon bar Samson and the Latin side through Albert of Aachen and Ekkehard of Aura (neutrality #11). The attackers' stated rationale (that the Jews were 'enemies of the Christian faith', in Albert's report, and the call to 'avenge the blood of "the hanged one"' that Solomon bar Samson puts in their mouths) is reported only as attributed language, never adopted; Solomon bar Samson's own register ('Emico the wicked') is likewise quoted as the chronicle's language. The Hebrew chronicles' understanding of martyrdom as kiddush ha-shem is described on its own terms as the communities' religious self-understanding, without editorial approval or criticism. Casualty figures for Mainz are attributed to the authors who give them (1,100 in Solomon bar Samson, about 700 in Albert) and none is adopted (neutrality #2). The Chazan and Cohen readings of the chronicles are presented as competing scholarly framings without adjudication. SOURCING: the Jewish primary lens is Solomon bar Samson in Jacob Marcus's translation (The Jew in the Medieval World, 1938), read directly on the Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook, and the Latin primary lens is Albert of Aachen and Ekkehard of Aura in Krey's 1921 translation, also read directly; both are rated high for the quoted passages. The full Hebrew corpus is cited through Eidelberg's English translation and Haverkamp's critical edition, and the academic lens through Chazan (1987) and Cohen (2004); these were verified to exist and be on-topic through publisher pages and library catalog records but were not read line-by-line, so they are rated medium. Claims resting only on them (the sequence and dates of the attacks at Speyer, Worms, and Cologne; Henry IV's permission of 1097; Ephraim of Bonn's account of 1146-1147) are therefore medium-confidence. No encyclopedias or tertiary sources are cited.

relations.note: The attacks were carried out by contingents gathering for the expedition proclaimed by Urban II at Clermont in 1095, before the main armies left for the East.
Rashi (1040-1105) had studied in the academies of Worms and Mainz, two of the communities attacked in 1096; he was living in Troyes at the time of the persecutions.
Ephraim of Bonn's Hebrew account of the persecutions during the Second Crusade (1146-1147), written in the tradition of the 1096 chronicles, records an attack on Rabbenu Tam at Ramerupt.

During the Second Crusade, Bernard of Clairvaux opposed the anti-Jewish preaching of the monk Radulf in the Rhineland, an intervention recorded in Ephraim of Bonn's Hebrew account of the persecutions of 1146-1147.
